title: Pasticciada Veneziana
subtitle: Venetian braised beef in wine and spices
excerpt: Pasticciada veneziana is a Venetian braised beef dish with a long history: beef marinated and then slowly braised in red wine with onions, celery, cloves, cinnamon, and vinegar. The sauce is rich and slightly sweet-sour from the spices, reflecting the medieval Venetian spice trade. It is traditionally served over polenta.
sourceNotes: Pasticciada veneziana is a historic Venetian dish documented since at least the seventeenth century. The spice combination -- cloves, cinnamon, nutmeg -- reflects Venice's role as the centre of the European spice trade. The dish is marinated overnight and braised slowly, making it a two-day preparation.

recipe.freezeNotes: Freeze the braised beef in its sauce. Reheat gently from frozen.
recipe.makeAheadNotes: Must marinate overnight. Improves if made a day ahead and reheated.

content.text: Pasticciada requires planning: the beef marinates overnight in wine, spices, and vinegar before braising. The marinade becomes the braising liquid. The long slow braise produces meat that falls apart and a sauce that is intensely spiced and rich. Serve over soft polenta or with mashed potato.

Place {{beef-brisket}} beef in a large bowl. Add {{red-wine}} wine, {{white-wine-vinegar}} vinegar, {{onion}} onion, {{celery}} celery, {{carrot}} carrot, and {{garlic}} garlic. Add {{cloves}} cloves, {{cinnamon-stick}} cinnamon, {{nutmeg}} nutmeg, and {{bay-leaves}} bay leaves. Cover and refrigerate for at least 8 hours, or overnight. Turn the beef once during the marinade.

Remove the beef from the marinade and pat dry. Reserve the marinade. Heat {{extra-virgin-olive-oil}} oil in a heavy pan over high heat. Brown the beef well on all sides, about 8 minutes total. Remove and set aside.

Pour the marinade and all its vegetables and spices into the pan. Bring to a boil and simmer for 5 minutes. Return the beef to the pan. Cover and cook at the lowest possible simmer for 2 to 2.5 hours until the beef is tender enough to cut with a spoon, turning it once. Season with {{salt-table}} salt.

Remove the beef and slice it thickly. Strain the sauce through a sieve, pressing the vegetables. Taste the sauce -- if too sharp, add a teaspoon of {{caster-sugar}} sugar. Return the beef slices and sauce to the pan to reheat. Serve over soft polenta or mashed potato.

items.cause: The vinegar has not been cooked out enough, or the wine is too sharp.
items.fix: Simmer the sauce for longer after straining to reduce and mellow the acidity. A teaspoon of sugar added to the sauce at the end is traditional in the Venetian version.

content.text: Pasticciada veneziana is one of the oldest dishes in Venetian cooking. The spice combination of cloves, cinnamon, and nutmeg reflects Venice's former role as the main entry point for spices from the east. The sweet-and-sour balance -- wine, vinegar, and a touch of sugar -- runs through Venetian cooking and appears in sarde in saor too. The dish is served at weddings and feast days across the Veneto.
